children: Halloween candy sales are declining as financially strained Americans cut back on discretionary purchases, with higher chocolate prices and rising household expenses weighing on demand ahead of the holiday.

U.S. candy sales fell 6.7% in the four weeks ended Oct. 17 from a year earlier, according to NielsenIQ data cited by the Associated Press. Sales had dropped 11.7% in mid-September, reversing the early-season gains recorded during the previous two years.

For investors, the slowdown signals mounting pressure on consumer spending and potential challenges for confectionery manufacturers, food retailers and other companies dependent on discretionary purchases. Weak demand despite some price reductions suggests households are increasingly prioritizing necessities, potentially limiting companies' ability to raise prices without sacrificing sales volumes.

Consumers have been squeezed by higher costs for gasoline, housing, groceries and clothing. The national average gasoline price reached $4.29 a gallon Friday, nearly 40% above its year-earlier level, according to the AP. NielsenIQ found that smaller candy packages were the only category showing sales growth through mid-October, while larger packages experienced the steepest declines.

Candy prices have substantially outpaced broader food inflation. Government data show that candy and gum prices climbed 44% over the five years through September, compared with a 22.5% increase in grocery prices. Discount retailer Aldi recently advertised a 135-piece assortment of Mars chocolate bars for $19.87, roughly what a 250-piece package cost five years earlier.

Cocoa prices have contributed to the increases. Futures reached a record $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 amid unfavorable weather in West Africa and speculative trading. Prices subsequently dropped to $3,241 in March before rebounding as the Iran war disrupted fertilizer supplies and forecasts of El Niño-related drought raised concerns about future production.

Lower prices haven't necessarily revived demand. Non-chocolate Halloween candy, including gummies and lollipops, averaged $6.08 per pound during the nine weeks ended Oct. 17, down about 3% from last year, according to NielsenIQ. Nevertheless, sales remained sluggish.

Industry analysts cautioned that consumers may be delaying purchases until closer to Halloween as they make smaller, more frequent shopping trips. The National Confectioners Association, which represents manufacturers including Mars and Ferrara Candy, remains optimistic that demand will strengthen during the final days before the holiday.
